:::{#rem-matrix-induced-inner-product-bilinear}
#### A symmetric bilinear form needs a positive definite matrix to be an inner product

@def-matrix-induced-inner-product uses the [symmetric bilinear form](linear-algebra-special-matrices.qmd#def-symmetric-bilinear-form) of $\matr{A}$ as an [inner product](linear-algebra-inner-products.qmd#def-inner-product)
only when $\matr{A}$ is also [positive definite](#def-positive-definite).
A [symmetric matrix](linear-algebra-special-matrices.qmd#def-symmetric-matrix) $\matr{A}$ that is not positive definite
has a nonzero vector $\vx$ with $\bformf{\matr{A}}{\vx}{\vx} \le 0$.
If $\bformf{\matr{A}}{\vx}{\vx} < 0$, the form breaks [positivity](linear-algebra-inner-products.qmd#def-inner-product-positivity);
if $\bformf{\matr{A}}{\vx}{\vx} = 0$, it breaks [definiteness](linear-algebra-inner-products.qmd#def-inner-product-definiteness).
Either way, that form is not an inner product.
For example, take $\matr{S}$ from @exm-symmetric-bilinear-form
and the vector $\vecf{z} = \tp{(1, -1)}$:

$$
\ba
\bformf{\matr{S}}{\vecf{z}}{\vecf{z}}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(@def-bilinear-form)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \cd 1 + 2 \cd (-1) \\ 2 \cd 1 + 1 \cd (-1) \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply the matrix by } \vecf{z} \text{)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply and add)}
\\
&= 1 \cd (-1) + (-1) \cd 1
&& \text{(multiply the row by the column)}
\\
&= -2.
&& \text{(multiply and add)}
\ea
$$

The [quadratic form](linear-algebra-special-matrices.qmd#def-quadratic-form) of $\matr{S}$ is negative at $\vecf{z}$,
so $\matr{S}$ is not positive definite.

:::
